blocks.text: To keep the conversation going, you should add more **details** and a **question**.

slides.tutorNotes:
Model the pattern: short answer, one extra detail, then a question back. 
Ask the student to answer the questions "Where are you from" and "What do you do?" using the same pattern.

Students at this level often stop after the first sentence (“I’m from Osaka.”). Praise any extra detail.

items: Where are you from? → I’m from Tokyo. ____
What do you do? → I’m a nurse. ____
Where do you live? → I live in Yokohama. ____
Would you like a cup of tea? → ____

blocks.title: Possible answers
blocks.text:
1. It’s the capital of Japan. And you?
2. I work in a big hospital. How about you?
3. It’s near Tokyo. Where do you live?
4. It’s big and exciting. Do you like it?
5. Nice to meet you, Ken!
6. Yes, please! / No, thanks. I’m fine.

slides.tutorNotes:
Any sensible answer is fine. The answers here are examples. (~2 min)
Watch for: “I from Tokyo” (missing am), “He is Ken” when introducing someone (use “This is Ken”) and the extra detail should be some information about Ken e.g, "He is..", and answering an offer with just “Yes.” (add “please”).

blocks.title: How it sounds
blocks.text:
Nice to meet you → nice ta **MEE**-choo

Where are you from? → wair-ra-ya **FROM**?

How about you? → how a-bou-**CHOO**?

slides.tutorNotes:
Say each line and wait for the student to repeat. the student repeats. (~1 min)
Make sure to say the assimilation 'choo' in 'meet you' and 'how about you'.
The spelling on the slide shows how the words join in natural speech: “to” becomes a weak “ta”, and “t” + “you” becomes “choo” (meet you → mee-choo, about you → a-bou-choo). 
In southern English accents the r in “where” is only heard when the next word starts with a vowel: wair-ra.
Capitals show the stressed word. In “Nice to meet you too”, the stress moves to TOO. In “How about you?”, stress YOU.

This is for listening and copying only, not spelling. Simply explain this is how native speakers talk.

header.label: Reading
header.title: Sharing a flat in the UK

blocks.alt: Photo idea: young flatmates chatting and cooking in a small shared kitchen

blocks.text:
Many young people in the UK live in a **flat** with **flatmates**. Rent in big cities like London is very expensive, so sharing is cheaper. Flatmates usually have their own bedroom, but they share the kitchen, the bathroom and the living room.

Flatmates are not always friends at the start. Often, they meet for the first time on moving day! Some flatmates cook and eat together. Others just say hello in the kitchen.

Some British people wear shoes inside the house, but many take them off at the door. And when someone new arrives, British people often offer them a cup of tea.

slides.tutorNotes:
The student reads aloud. Correct pronunciation gently at the end. Wait for the student to read the entire text. (~2.5 min)
Check: Why do people share flats? What do flatmates share? What do British people often offer a new person?

blocks.title: Why Friday?
blocks.text:
Lots of British people eat fish and chips on Friday. Why? 
A long time ago, many Christians didn’t eat meat on Fridays, so they ate fish. Some people also say workers got paid on Friday, so they bought dinner at the chip shop.

blocks.text: Sunday, one o’clock. Haruka goes to **Gwen’s** flat. Tom is there too.

lines.speaker: Gwen
lines.text: Hello, love! Come in, come in.

lines.speaker: Haruka
lines.text: Thank you, Mrs Davies. This is for you. It’s a small gift from Osaka.

lines.speaker: Gwen

blocks.text: Use these words to say how often you do something.

blocks.text:
__Frequency words__

__Phrases at the end__

blocks.title: Three sounds for ’s
blocks.text: Kate**’s** → **s**     Tom**’s**, Gwen**’s** → **z**     George**’s** → **iz**

slides.tutorNotes:
Say each name, the student repeats. Many learners drop the final ’s, so make it clear and a little long. (~1 min)
The rule: “s” after p, t, k, f sounds (Kate’s, Jack’s). “z” after vowels and most other sounds (Tom’s, Gwen’s, Haruka’s). “iz” after s, z, sh, ch, j sounds (George’s, Grace’s).
Don’t add an extra vowel: Tom’s is one beat, not “Tomuzu”.

blocks.alt: Photo idea: Yorkshire puddings and roast potatoes with gravy

blocks.text:
On Sundays, many families in the UK eat a big lunch together. It’s called a **Sunday roast**. There is roast meat (usually chicken, beef, lamb or pork), roast potatoes, vegetables and **gravy**. Many people also have **Yorkshire puddings**. They aren’t sweet!

Some families have a roast every week. Others have one once a month, or only on special days. You can also have a Sunday roast in a lot of pubs.

Each meat often has its own sauce: mint sauce with lamb, apple sauce with pork, and horseradish sauce (hot and spicy) with beef. And after lunch? Many people have a **pudding**, or just a cup of tea!

blocks.alt: Photo idea: a friend bringing a round of drinks to a pub table

blocks.text:
British people say **sorry** a lot. They say it when they make a mistake, but not only then. If someone walks into you, you might both say sorry! People also say “Sorry?” when they didn’t hear something.

In a pub, you usually order and pay at the **bar**. There usually isn’t a proper queue, but the staff try to serve people in order. Don’t shout or wave at them. Just wait, and smile when they look at you.

Friends often buy drinks in **rounds**. One person buys drinks for everyone. Then the next person buys the next round. Always buy your round!

blocks.alt: Photo idea: a full English seen from above

blocks.text:
A **full English**, or a **fry-up**, is a big, hot breakfast. It usually has eggs, bacon, sausages, baked beans, mushrooms, tomatoes and toast. Some cafés also add black pudding. It’s a sausage made with pork blood, fat and oats.

It’s a big meal, so many people have it at the weekend, not every day. People often drink a cup of tea with it, and add ketchup or brown sauce.

Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have their own version, with different breads and extras.

blocks.alt: Photo idea: fireworks over a park on Bonfire Night

blocks.text:
Every year on 5 November, people in Britain celebrate **Bonfire Night**. In 1605, a group of men, including Guy Fawkes, planned to blow up the Houses of Parliament. Their plan failed, and people lit bonfires to celebrate.

Today, families go to big **fireworks** displays in parks. Some people put a model of Guy Fawkes, called a “guy”, on top of the **bonfire**. People eat **toffee apples** and hold **sparklers**. There is a famous rhyme British people say for this holiday: “Remember, remember, the fifth of November.”

It’s usually cold, so everyone wears hats, scarves and gloves.

slides.tutorNotes: Quick check. If the student can’t answer, go back to the dialogue together. (~1 min)

blocks.alt: Photo idea: someone smiling and giving a thumbs-up in the rain

blocks.text:
Gwen said “Lovely weather, isn’t it?” on a rainy day. She didn’t mean it! This is **sarcasm**: saying the opposite of what you actually mean.

You’ll often hear people in Britain joke like this about small problems, like bad weather or a long queue. It’s friendly, not rude. The other person often joins in: “Oh yes, perfect weather for the beach!”

How can you tell? Look at the situation. If it’s raining and someone says “lovely”, they’re using sarcasm. Just smile, or make a joke back.

slides.tutorNotes:
Read together right after the first dialogue, so the joke makes sense. (~2 min)
Check: Did Gwen really think the weather was lovely? What is sarcasm? How can you tell when someone is joking?
Background: Kate Fox (Watching the English) describes irony as a constant part of English conversation. Ask the student: do people in Japan joke like this? When?
Also: weather is a safe topic for small talk in Britain because it changes a lot and everyone can join in.

blocks.title: Tongue between your teeth
blocks.text:
Soft **th**: **th**anks · **th**ink · **Th**ursday

With your voice: **th**e · **th**an · wea**th**er

Not s or z: **th**ink ≠ sink · **th**ank ≠ sank

slides.tutorNotes:
Show the student your tongue between your teeth, then blow air out. (~1 min)
Japanese learners often replace th with s or z (“sank you”, “zey”) or with d. The soft th (think) has no voice; the th in the, than and weather has voice: touch your throat to feel it.
Comparatives from today use a lot of th: than, the, weather.

blocks.text:

blocks.text:

blocks.title: a, the or – (nothing)?
Answers
blocks.text:
1. a (one of many)
2. the (we both know which)
3. the (line names)
4. a (first time)
5. The (only one)
6. – (by train)

slides.tutorNotes:
The student chooses a, the or nothing (–), and says why. Articles are hard for Japanese learners because Japanese doesn’t have them, so keep it short and come back to it when you hear mistakes. (~2 min)
Simple rules:
• a / an: one of many, or the first time you mention it (a café, a red phone box).
• the: we both know which one, or there’s only one (the station near here, the Tube). Tube and Underground lines use the (the Northern line).
• nothing: by train, by bus, at home, go to work.

blocks.title: First conditional
blocks.text:

**If you take** the Northern line, …

__will + verb__

… **you’ll get** there in twenty minutes.

__Careful__

**If you get** lost, call me. (not “If you will get”)

blocks.title: Two different sounds
blocks.text:
**L**: your tongue touches behind your top teeth → **l**eft · **l**ine · p**l**atform

**R**: your tongue doesn’t touch anything → **r**ight · **r**ed · t**r**ain

**l**ight ≠ **r**ight · **l**ong ≠ w**r**ong

slides.tutorNotes:
Let the student watch your mouth. Practise the pairs slowly, then fast. (~1 min)
Japanese ら行 sounds are between English l and r, so both can be hard. For l, the tongue touches behind the top teeth; for r, the lips round a little and the tongue touches nothing.
In many English accents (including London), an r at the end of a word isn’t pronounced: Northern = NOR-thn, car = KAH. Scottish accents do pronounce it, so listen to Callum! Directions use left and right all the time, so this matters today.

blocks.text: Saturday afternoon. Priya and Haruka are in a tea room in the Cotswolds.

lines.speaker: Haruka
lines.text: Is this afternoon tea? It’s on my list!

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Not quite. This is a cream tea: tea, **scones**, **clotted cream** and **jam**.

lines.speaker: Haruka
lines.text: OK! Jam first, or cream first?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Careful! In Devon, it’s cream first. In Cornwall, it’s jam first.

lines.speaker: Haruka
lines.text: And in the Cotswolds?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Here? Nobody minds. Just enjoy it!

lines.speaker: Haruka
lines.text: Mmm! This is better than any cake in London!

slides.tutorNotes:
Read once together (student = Haruka), then swap roles. (~2 min)
A cream tea is a simple kind of afternoon tea. People in Devon and Cornwall really do argue about the order of cream and jam. Haruka counts it as “afternoon tea” on her UK list.
Recycles “better than” from Lesson 5. Ask: Which would you put first, and why?
This is Saturday afternoon. That evening Haruka tells her brother about the day.

blocks.title: Answers
blocks.text: 1. Tea, scones, clotted cream and jam.  2. Not quite: it’s a simple kind.  3. In Devon.  4. Yes: it’s better than any cake in London!

blocks.title: Past simple
blocks.text:
__Regular (-ed)__

visit → **visited** · walk → **walked** · miss → **missed**

__Irregular__

go → **went** · take → **took** · catch → **caught** · be → **was / were**

__Negative__

We **didn’t catch** the bus. (not “didn’t caught”)

items: Haruka: Then I **took** lots of photos for you.
blocks.title: From the story

blocks.text: Use the past simple for finished events, like last weekend.

slides.tutorNotes:
Japanese learners often add -ed to irregular verbs (“goed”) or keep the past form after didn’t (“didn’t went”). (~1.5 min)
Pronunciation of -ed comes on the pronunciation slide.

blocks.title: Answers
blocks.text:
1. went
2. visited
3. had
4. were
5. missed
6. didn’t catch

slides.tutorNotes: The student completes each sentence with the past simple, then retells Haruka’s Saturday without looking. (~1.5 min)

blocks.title: Past questions and sequencers
blocks.text:
__Questions__

Where **did** you **go**? · What **did** you **do**? · How **did** you **get** home?

__Telling a story__

**First**, … · **Then** … · **After that**, … · **In the end**, …

__Answers__

We went to Lacock. (not “We did go”)
Use did to ask about the past, and first, then, after that to tell a story in order.

slides.tutorNotes:
Questions in the past use did + the base verb. Sequencers make a story easy to follow. (~1.5 min)
Watch for: “Where you went?” (no did) and “What did you went?”.

blocks.title: Example answer
blocks.text: First, I met my friend in Umeda. Then we had lunch. After that, we went shopping. In the end, I got home at nine!

slides.tutorNotes: Ask each question. The student answers in the past simple, and uses first, then, after that in at least one answer. Skip this slide if time is short. (~1.5 min)

blocks.title: How it sounds
blocks.text:
walked → **WOKT**   stayed → **STAYD**   visited → **VIZ**-it-id
What did you do? → wot dija **DOO**?
Where did you go? → wair dija **GO**?

items: What did you **do** at the weekend?
blocks.title: Say it with your teacher

slides.tutorNotes:
Say each word, the student repeats. (~1 min)
The -ed ending has three sounds: “t” after p, k, s, sh, ch (walked, missed); “d” after most other sounds (stayed, played); “id” after t and d (visited, wanted). Don’t add a vowel: walked is one beat, not “wokudo”.
“Did you” joins into “dija”.

blocks.text:
The UK is a small country, but it has lots of different **accents**. People from Manchester, Liverpool, Glasgow and London can sound very different, even when they use the same words.

Don’t worry if you don’t understand everything. British people often ask each other to repeat things too!

blocks.text:
__Questions__

**Have** you **ever been** to a gig? · **Have** you **seen** Oasis?

Yes, I **have**. I**’ve been** to lots. · No, I **haven’t**. I**’ve never seen** them.

be → **been** · see → **seen** · hear → **heard** · eat → **eaten**

blocks.text:
A **gig** is an informal word for a live music concert. In the UK, many gigs are in small **venues**, like pubs and clubs. Often there are no seats. Everyone stands, and the people who arrive first get the best places near the **stage**.

Many famous bands started in small venues. The Beatles came from Liverpool, and Oasis came from Manchester. In 2025, Oasis played together again for the first time in 16 years, and millions of fans tried to get tickets.

Before the main band, there is often a **support act**. In 2026 the Japanese band 'Otoboke Beaver' were a support act for the Foo Fighters in Liverpool's Anfield Stadium!

blocks.text: August. Callum meets Haruka and Kenta at Edinburgh Waverley station.

lines.speaker: Callum
lines.text: Welcome to Edinburgh! You must be Kenta.

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.text: Hi, Callum! Nice to meet you. Wow, it’s so busy!

lines.speaker: Callum
lines.text: Aye, it’s the Fringe. Have you ever been to a festival like this?

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.text: No, never! What should we see first?

lines.speaker: Callum
lines.text: The castle. It’s on an old volcano, right in the middle of the city.

lines.speaker: Haruka
lines.text: A volcano? Is it safe?

lines.speaker: Callum
lines.text: Don’t worry. It stopped millions of years ago!

slides.tutorNotes:
Read once together (student = Haruka or Kenta), then swap roles. (~2 min)

Edinburgh Castle stands on Castle Rock, the remains of a volcano that was active around 350 million years ago.
This dialogue recycles “You must be…” (Lesson 1), “Aye” (Lesson 9), the present perfect (Lesson 10) and should (Lesson 11).

blocks.title: Answers
blocks.text: 1. At Edinburgh Waverley station.  2. It’s the Fringe.  3. The castle.  4. An old volcano.

slides.tutorNotes: Quick check. If the student can’t answer, go back to the dialogue together. (~1 min)

blocks.text: The next morning. Haruka and Kenta are at the top of Arthur’s Seat.

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.text: What a **view**! So, how was your year in London?

lines.speaker: Haruka
lines.text: Amazing! I’ve done everything on my list.

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.text: Everything? Have you had a full English?

lines.speaker: Haruka
lines.text: Yes, and I’ve eaten black pudding! I’ve been to Bonfire Night and pulled a Christmas cracker.

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.text: And now you’ve climbed a volcano! Are you sad to go home next month?

lines.speaker: Haruka
lines.text: Actually… my boss asked me to stay another year.

lines.speaker: Kenta
lines.text: Really? What are you going to do?

slides.tutorNotes:
Read together. (~2 min)
Haruka looks back on the whole course: full English (Lesson 4), black pudding, Bonfire Night (Lesson 5), Christmas cracker (Lesson 6). Ask the student which of these they would like to try.
Kenta’s question is the big question of the course. Ask the student: What do you think Haruka will do?

blocks.title: Present perfect or past simple?
blocks.text:
__Your life so far__

I**’ve done** everything on my list. · I**’ve eaten** black pudding.

__A finished time__

I **ate** black pudding **in October**. · We **climbed** it **this morning**.

__Telling your news__

I**’ve decided to** learn more English! · I**’ve got** some news.

Kenta: And now **you’ve climbed** a volcano!
blocks.title: From the story

blocks.text: Use the present perfect for your life so far, and the past simple for a finished time.

slides.tutorNotes: Review, not new grammar. Keep it to the simple rule: life so far → present perfect; a finished time → past simple. (~1.5 min)

2. some (L4)

slides.tutorNotes: A quick review of grammar from every unit. The student completes each sentence, then makes their own example. (~2 min)

blocks.title: Strong words, quick words
blocks.text:
Put stress on the important words: I’ve **DONE EV**erything on my **LIST**.

Say the small words quickly without stress: I’ve, on, my, to, a, the.

This makes your English sound natural and clear.

slides.tutorNotes:
Clap the stressed words while you say each line; the small words fit between the claps. (~1 min)
English has a regular beat: the important words are strong, and the small words are quick and weak. Japanese gives each syllable a similar length, so English can sound flat without this.
Review: ask the student which pronunciation point from the course was the hardest, and practise it once more.

blocks.text: That evening. Haruka video-calls her mum in Osaka.

lines.speaker: Haruka
lines.text: Mum, I’ve got some news. My company wants me to stay another year.

lines.speaker: Mum
lines.text: Another year? But we **miss** you!

lines.speaker: Haruka
lines.text: I miss you too. But I love my job, and my English is much better.

lines.speaker: Mum
lines.text: It sounds great! So, what do you want to do?

lines.speaker: Haruka
lines.text: I want to stay. But I wanted to talk to you first.

lines.speaker: Mum
lines.text: Haruka, it’s your life. If you’re happy, we’re happy.

lines.speaker: Haruka
lines.text: Thank you, Mum. I’ll come home for New Year!

slides.tutorNotes:
Read together. In real life they speak Japanese; the dialogue is in English for practice. (~1.5 min)
New Year is the big family holiday in Japan (Lesson 6), so coming home for New Year matters.
Ask: Would you talk to your family first, like Haruka? Why?

blocks.text:

• Give advice: Should she stay or go home?
• Use if… will: “If you stay, you’ll…”

blocks.title: Teacher
blocks.text:
You’re Haruka. Use the story.

• Talk about your year: work, Tom, Gwen.
• Say what you miss about Japan.
• Ask: “Should I stay or go home?”

slides.tutorNotes: Do it once. The teacher is Haruka and uses what happened in the course (her job, Tom, Gwen, tea). The student is her friend and gives advice. Encourage should, if… will, and the present perfect. (~2.5 min)

blocks.title: Student
blocks.text:
Talk to your teacher about your year.

• What have you done? Who have you met?
• Tell one story: first, then, in the end.
• What are you going to do next?

blocks.title: Teacher
blocks.text:
Ask about the student’s year.

• Ask “Have you ever…?” and “What happened?”
• Ask about their plans.
• Give one piece of advice.

slides.tutorNotes:
Final check for the whole course. Let the student lead and don’t correct during the conversation. Note what they do well and one thing to practise. (~3 min)
Look for: introductions and asking back, polite requests, comparing, plans with be + -ing, telling a story in the past, the present perfect for experiences, should and have to. The student self-checks on the wrap-up slide.

blocks.alt: Photo idea: the Royal Mile during the Fringe

blocks.text:
Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland. Its famous **castle** stands on a rock that was once a **volcano**. Arthur’s Seat, another old volcano in the city, is 251 metres high, and the **view** from the top is amazing.

The Royal Mile is the old street between the castle and the Palace of Holyroodhouse.

Every August, the city has the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, the world’s biggest arts festival. Thousands of shows happen all over the city, and the Royal Mile is full of **street performers**.

slides.tutorNotes:
The student reads aloud. Correct pronunciation at the end of each paragraph. (~2.5 min)
Check: What is the castle built on? How high is Arthur’s Seat? When is the Fringe?
Sources: Edinburgh Castle (Castle Rock is a volcanic plug); Arthur’s Seat 251 m; Edinburgh Festival Fringe (since 1947, every August).

blocks.text: Back in London. Haruka has a cup of tea with Gwen and Tom.

lines.speaker: Gwen
lines.text: So, how was Edinburgh, love?

lines.speaker: Haruka
lines.text: Wonderful! And I’ve got some news. **I’ve decided** to stay another year!

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Yes! So I don’t need a new flatmate!

lines.speaker: Gwen
lines.text: Oh, that’s lovely. Let’s **celebrate**. I’ll put the kettle on!

lines.speaker: Haruka
lines.text: Can I put the milk in first?

lines.speaker: Gwen
lines.text: Absolutely not!

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Haha! Some things never change.

slides.tutorNotes:
